impossible to discover whether the voice was recognised or not ; the numbers being so even, I shall perhaps be justified in assigning 2 of these to one class, and 2 to the other. The computation will be clearer if we consider only the cases in which the voice was recognised, and the person whom it suggested was living ; these, then may be taken as 33. But, out of the 33 persons, 10^1 profess to have had the experience more than once. Such cases of repetition, or at any rate most of them, might fairly have been disregarded ; for since the large majority of the persons who have had one of the coincidental hallucinations, which appear later in the calculation, can recall no other hallucination besides that one, I might in the same proportion confine the present list, which consists wholly of non-coincidental or purely subjective hallucinations, to similarly unique experiences, and leave out of account those occurring to people who seem rather more pre-disposed to such affections. However, in order to make ample allowance for the possibility that the witnesses in the coincidental cases may have had subjective hallucinations which they have forgotten, let us take the repetitions into account ; and let us suppose each of the 10 persons just mentioned to have had 4 experiences of the sort within the specified 12 years. The most convenient way of making this allowance will be to add 30 to the former total of 33—i.e., to take the number of persons who have had the experience under the given conditions as 63. This amounts to 1 in every 90 of the group of 5705 persons named, or (if that group be accepted as fairly representative of the population of this country) 1 in every 90 of the population.

Let us now see what the proportion of the population who have had such an experience ought to be, on the hypothesis that the similar impressions of recognised voices presented in this book as telepathic were really chance-coincidences. As before in the case of dreams (Vol. I., pp. 303-7), I take cases where the coincidence of the hallucination was with death—the reasons for this selection being (1) that death is the prominent event in our telepathic cases ; and (2) that for the purpose of an accurate numerical estimate it is important to select an event of a very definite and unmistakeable kind, such as only happens once to each individual. Again also, in accordance with the official returns which give 22/1000 as the annual death-rate, the proportion of anyone’s relatives and acquaintances

phantasms_52.translation:
<page-num>20</page-num>
<header>THE THEORY OF CHANCE-COINCIDENCE. [CHAP.</header>

other words, unless purely subjective hallucinations were 1023^1
times as numerous as my census shows them to be. But it must be
further remembered that Mr. S.’s case was drawn from a very incon-
siderable fraction of the adult population—a fraction which it was
extravagantly liberal to estimate at one-eightieth; and even if we
ourselves knew of no other like it, the presumption would be that the
seventy-nine eightieths of the population to which we have obtained
no access could supply parallel instances. But in fact the case
is very far from standing alone even in our collection. Taking only
the "borderland" and waking phantasms, recorded on first-hand
testimony in the main body of this work, I find that 66 of them are
represented as having occurred within an hour of the event on the
agent's side—which event in 41 of the 66 cases was death; 15 more,
according to the facts stated, were within two hours of the event,
which in 10 of the 15 cases was death; and in nearly all these cases,
as well as in several others, it is quite possible that the coincidence
was absolutely exact. I do not forget, what I have expressly pointed out
in Chap. IV., that exaggeration of the closeness of the coincidence is a
likely form for exaggeration in such matters to take ;^2 but in a con-
siderable number of the cases mentioned, good reason is shown for
believing it to have been as close as is stated. Moreover, the appli-
cation of the scheme just used to the whole body of less exact
coincidences, would give for each one of them in turn a less enormous,
but still an enormous improbability that it was due to chance.
The improbability, therefore, that only chance has been at work is in
reality immensely in excess of what the numbers given would
suggest: it is the cumulation of numerous improbabilities, each of
which is enormous.

But the huge total of improbability is nothing like complete.
Nothing has been said of the aggregate strength of the cases where
the phantasm was unrecognised. Nothing has been said of the large
array of cases where the coincident event was not death, but some
other form of crisis—a class which does not lend itself easily to a
precise numerical estimate, but whose collective force, even if it stood

^1 This number is derived thus. Having found from the census that those who have had a visual hallucination of the type in question in 12 years amount to about 1 in every 248, we may fairly suppose those who have had such an experience in a generation to be about 2½ times as numerous, or 1 in 99 of the population. If the adult population be reckoned as 24 millions, this would give about 242,424 hallucinations of the type in question in a generation—i. e. about 1/1023 of the 248 millions which the chance theory would imply.
^2 Thus it would be quite unjustifiable to add to the list a number of cases in the Supplement where the coincidence is stated to have been exact. Still the Supplement contains several accounts—e. g., Nos. 508, 510, 569, 584, 599—which may fairly be assumed to be correct in this particular.

kepler_an_158.note: Translation opens with a markdown running head, a margin note, then "...the hypothesis"; the Latin opens "(bisecta scilicet…". The page ends on a full stop (the catchword "Sed cum" starts a new sentence).
kepler_an_158.translation:
# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE STAR MARS

<margin>CHAP. XIX.</margin>
...the hypothesis found in Chapter 16 (specifically by <term>bisecting the eccentricity<gloss>splitting the total distance between the Sun and the point of uniform motion into two equal parts to place the center of the orbit</gloss></term>). Now, because they could not be ignored, these eight minutes of arc alone led the way to the reformation of all ASTRONOMY, and they have become the subject matter for a great part of this WORK.

CHAPTER XX.

Refutation of that same hypothesis by observations made outside of acronychal positions.

NOW I shall proceed to a second argument by which the "eccentric eccentricity" found in Chapter 17 is shown to be false (notwithstanding the fact that it provides the true motions in longitude): namely, by using observations of other configurations with the Sun made outside of <term>oppositions<gloss>when Mars is directly opposite the Sun from Earth's perspective</gloss></term>, specifically when the planet was observed while moving near the <term>apsides<gloss>the points where the planet is closest to or farthest from the Sun</gloss></term> of the <term>eccentric<gloss>the circular path of the planet</gloss></term>.

In the year 1600, on March 5/15, around midnight, Mars was seen at 29° 12' 30'' in Cancer (♋) with a latitude of 3° 23' North. Its mean longitude, corrected by our addition, was 4 signs, 29° 14' 58''; its <term>aphelion<gloss>the point in the orbit furthest from the Sun</gloss></term> was at 4 signs, 29° 2' 45''. Therefore, the <term>anomaly<gloss>the angle measuring the planet's progress around its orbit from its furthest point</gloss></term> was 0° 12' 13''. This requires an <term>equation<gloss>a correction added or subtracted to the mean motion to find the true position</gloss></term> of 2' to be subtracted, according to the hypothesis of eccentric positions established above. Therefore, the eccentric position of Mars was at 29° 13' Cancer; the Sun's position was at 25° 45' 51'' Aries (♈).

*In the diagram, let A be the Sun, B Mars, and C Earth. Therefore, by subtracting the direction of the Earth from Mars (CB = 29° 12' 30'' Cancer) from the direction of the Sun to Mars (AB = 29° 13' Cancer), the angle CBA will be 0° 30' 30''. By subtracting the direction of the Sun from the Earth (CA = 25° 45' 51'' Aries) from the direction of Mars from the Earth (CB = 29° 12' 30'' Cancer), the angle BCA will be 123° 26' 39''. Now, as the sine of angle CBA is to the side CA, so is the sine of angle BCA to the side BA. However, CA (the distance of the Sun from the Earth according to Tycho's tables) is 99,302 (which, although slightly flawed, the true value lies within 100,000, as we shall hear below in Chapter 30). Therefore, the distance AB is between 165,680 and 166,846.*

Let us take an observation at <term>perihelion<gloss>the point in the orbit closest to the Sun</gloss></term>, which was held in the year 1593 on July 30, at 1:45 AM the following night. Mars was found at 17° 39' Aries (♈) with a latitude of 6° 6' 15'' South. The mean longitude of Mars was 1 sign, 26° 16' 38''. The aphelion was at 4 signs, 28° 55' 43''. Therefore, Mars is distant from the perihelion by 2° 39' 5'', to which an equation of 32' to be subtracted corresponds, according to the hypothesis found above, so that the eccentric position of Mars is 1 sign, 25° 44' 30'', and the apparent position of the Sun is 17° 3' 0'' Leo (♌).

*In the diagram, let BA be extended to D; let AD be at 25° 44' 30'' Aquarius (♒), and ED at 17° 39' 30'' Aries (♈). Therefore, angle EDA is 21° 55' 0''. And because ED is at 17° 39' 30'' Aries, and EA is at 17° 3' Leo, the angle AED is 149° 23' 30''. As the sine of angle EDA is to side EA, so is the sine of angle AED to side AD. Now, EA (the distance of the Sun from the Earth from Tycho's table) is 102,689—flawed indeed, but certainly greater than 100,000. Therefore, the distance AD is between 140,080 and 136,409.*

ksemaraja_38.note: Translation opens with an untagged mixed-case running head, then "...Such performance". Original is Devanagari.
ksemaraja_38.translation:
Pratyabhijñā-Hṛdayam [Sutra 12]

...Such performance of the five-fold acts, though always present for everyone, does not shine forth without the instruction of a <term>sadguru</term>. Therefore, one should follow the path of the true teacher for this recognition. || 11 ||

For one who does not have this knowledge without the instruction of a true teacher, there occurs a state of being deluded by one’s own powers, whose nature is covered over. He says:

> By not knowing this, one is deluded by one’s own powers, which is the state of being a worldly being. || 12 ||

"Of this"—of the constant possibility of this performance of the five-fold acts—in the "non-knowledge," that is, in the non-shining forth due to the absence of the unfolding of one’s own power caused by the descent of grace (<term>śaktipāta</term>), the "being deluded by one’s own powers"—being pierced by the stakes of various worldly and scriptural doubts—is precisely what is called "the state of a worldly being." This is stated in the <term>Śrī-Sarvavīrabhaṭṭāraka</term> scripture:

र्वस्य सदा संनिहितमपि सद्गुरूपदेशं विना न प्रकाशते, इति सद्गुरुपर्यैव एतत्प्रथार्थम् अनुसर्तव्या ॥ ११ ॥

यस्य पुनः सद्गुरूपदेशं विना एतत्परिज्ञानं नास्ति, तस्य अवच्छादितस्वरूपामिः निजामिः शक्तिभिः व्यामोहितत्वं भवति ।—इत्याह

> तदपरिज्ञाने स्वशक्तिभिर्व्यामोहितता संसारित्वम् ॥ १२ ॥

‘तस्य’ एतस्य सदा संभवतः पञ्चविधकृत्यकारित्वस्य ‘अपरिज्ञाने’—शक्तिपातहेतुकस्वबलोन्मीलनाभावात् अप्रकाशने ‘स्वाभिः शक्तिभिर्व्यामोहितत्वं’—विविधलौकिकशास्त्रीयशङ्काशङ्कुकीलितत्वं यत्, इदमेव ‘संसारित्वम्’ । तदुक्तं श्रीसर्ववीरभट्टारके

पं० २ क. पु० सद्गुरूपसस्यवेति; अनुमन्तव्येति च पाठः ।
पं० ५ क. पु० तस्य छादितस्वरूपामिः इति पाठः; निजामिः इति पदं ङ. पुस्तकादुपक्षिप्तम् ।
पं० ६ ग. पु० शक्तिव्यामोहितत्वं संसारित्वमित्याहेति पाठः ।
पं० ७ ख. पु० स्वशक्तिव्यामोहितता इति, ङ. पु० शक्तिव्यामोहितत्वम् इति पाठः ।
पं० ९ क. ग. पु० तदा इति पाठः ।

plotinus_101.translation:
LIBER SEXTVS. 57

[Right Column - Latin Text]

A ...fleeing to our sweet homeland. What then is the method of fleeing? And by what way shall we avoid the enchantments of Circe and Calypso? This, indeed, the very obscure fable of Ulysses signifies: which feigns him unwilling to remain, although pleasant spectacles met his eyes, and other things which are offered to the senses were promised. But our homeland is there, whence we came, and there also f[unclear] [unclear] a 101 ett, whence we came....

B Father. What then is the fleet, and what is the flight? Certainly, it is not to be fled by foot. For feet carry one from one land to another everywhere. Nor again ought we to prepare horses for riding, nor ships for sailing for this purpose: nay rather, to dismiss all these things, and not even to look forward, but with the sight of the body closed, to assume and awaken another sight in place of this. Which indeed all possess, but very few use.

ἄναγε ἐπὶ σαυτὸν καὶ ἴδε, κἂν μήπω σαυτὸν ἴδῃς καλὸν, οἷα ποιητὴς ἀγάλματος, ὃ δεῖ καλὸν γενέσθαι, τὸ μὲν ἀφαιρεῖ, τὸ δὲ ἀπέξεσε, τὸ δὲ λεῖον, τὸ δὲ καθαρὸν ἐποίησεν, ἕως ἔδειξε καλὸν ἐπὶ τῷ ἀγάλματι πρόσωπον. <margin>D</margin> οὕτω καὶ σὺ ἀφαίρει ὅσα περιττὰ, καὶ ἀπεύθυνε ὅσα σκολιὰ, ὅσα σκοτεινὰ καθαίρων, ἐργάζου εἶναι λαμπρὰ, καὶ μὴ παύσῃ τεκταίνων τὸ σὸν ἄγαλμα, ἕως ἂν ἐκλάμψειέ σοι τῆς ἀρετῆς ἡ θεοειδὴς ἀγλαΐα, ἕως ἂν ἴδοις σωφροσύνην, ἐν ἁγνῷ βεβῶσαν βάθρῳ. εἰ γέγονας τοῦτο, καὶ εἶδες αὐτὸ, καὶ σαυτῷ καθαρῶς συνεγένου, οὐδὲν ἔχων ἐμπόδιον <margin>E</margin> πρὸς τὸ, εἷς οὕτω γενέσθαι, οὐδὲ σὺν αὐτῷ ἄλλο τι ἐντὸς μεμιγμένον ἔχων, ἀλλ’ ὅλος αὐτὸς φῶς ἀληθινὸν μόνον, οὐ μεγέθει μεμετρημένον, οὐδὲ σχήματί τινι ἐλάττονι περιγραφὲν, οὐδ’ αὖ εἰς μέγεθος δι’ ἀπειρίας αὐξηθέν, <margin>*ἰσότητος <unclear>μεμ...</unclear></margin> ἀλλὰ ἀμέτρητον πανταχοῦ, ὡς ἂν μεῖζον παντὸς μέτρου, καὶ παντὸς κρεῖσσον ποσοῦ· εἰ <margin>F</margin> τοῦτο γενόμενος σαυτὸν ἴδοις, ὄψις ἤδη γενόμενος, θαρσήσας περὶ σαυτῷ καὶ ἐνταῦθα ἤδη ἀναβεβηκὼς, μηκέτι τοῦ δεικνύντος δεηθείς, ἀτενίσας ἴδε· τοῦτο γὰρ μόνον ὁ ὀφθαλμὸς τὸ μέγα κάλλος βλέπει. ἐὰν δὲ ἐπὶ τὴν θέαν λημῶν κακίαις, καὶ οὐ κεκα<margin>*ἀνανδρία</margin>θαρμένος, ἢ ἀσθενὴς *ἀνδρίᾳ οὐ δυνάμενος τὰ πάνυ λαμπρὰ βλέπειν, οὐδὲν βλέπει, κἂν ἄλλος δεικνύῃ παρόν, τὸ ὁραθῆναι δυνάμενον. τὸ γὰρ ὁρῶν πρὸς τὸ ὁρώμενον συγγενὲς καὶ ὅμοιον ποιη<margin>G</margin>σάμενον, δεῖ ἐπιβάλλειν τῇ θέᾳ. οὐ γὰρ ἂν πώποτε εἶδεν ὀφθαλμὸς ἥλιον, ἡλιοειδὴς μὴ γεγενημένος· οὐδὲ τὸ καλὸν ἂν ἴδῃ ψυχὴ μὴ καλὴ γενομένη. γενέσθω δὴ πρῶτον θεοειδὴς πᾶς, καὶ καλὸς πᾶς, εἰ μέλλει θεάσασθαι θεόν τε καὶ καλόν. ἥξει γὰρ πρῶτον ἀναβαίνων ἐπὶ τὸν νοῦν.

patriam dulcem confugientes. Quęnam igitur fugiendi ratio? & qua via veneficia Circes, Calypsúsque deuitabimus? Quod quidem licet perobſcura Vlixis ſignificat fabula: quæ illum fingit manere nolentem: quamuis ſpectacula illi oculis iucunda occurrerent: & cæteræ quæ ſe obiectant, promitterentur. Patria verò noſtra eſt, vnde venimus, ibidem quoque pater. Quęnā igitur claſſis, & quæ fuga? Haud ſanè pedibus eſt fugiendum. Pedes enim ab alia paſſim in aliam ferunt terram. Neque rurſus equos ad vehēdum: neque naues ad nauigandum huius gratia parare debemus: imò verò hæc cuncta dimitterere, neque proſpicere quidem, ſed viſu corporis clauſo alterum pro hoc viſum aſſumere, atque ſuſcitare. Quem habent quidem omnes: vtuntur verò perpauci.

<margin>IX Quomodo anima eandẽ ad verã pulchritudinẽ perueniat, & qualis illa pulchritudo.</margin> Quidnam igitur intimus ille oculus inſpicit? Profectò ſubitò experrectus haud valdè lucida poteſt aſpicere. Aſſuefaciēdus igitur animus primò quidem ſtudia pulchra conſiderare, deinde opera pulchra: opera, inquam, nō quæ fiunt ab artibus, ſed quæ à viris probis aguntur: poſt hæc eorum animum qui talia gerunt debes inſpicere. Quónam igitur pacto quale ſit animi bōni decus inſpicies? Age, te reuoca in te ipſum, atque contemplare, ac ſi nōdum te cognoſces pulchrum, ſtatuarium imitabere. Hic enim vbi ſtatuam optat pulchram, partim quidem abſcindit, partim quoque dirigit, & expolitus abradit, partim leuigat & abſtergit, donec faciem in ſtatua exprimat ſpecioſam. Ita & tu tolle ſuperuacua: obliqua dirige: obſcura purgando colluſtra: neque deſinas circa ſtatuam tuam elaborare, quouſque diuinus virtutis fulgor tibi ſubrutilet, quoad temperantiam cernas firmiter in maieſtate pura ſanctáque ſedentem. Si hoc ipſum euaſeris, atque ipſum ſimulque teipſum inſpexeris, ac purus iam habitaueris ipſe tecum, nihil videlicet habens impedimenti, quò minus ſic vnus efficiaris: neque rurſus habens aliud quicquam tecum intus admiſtum, ſed totus ipſe verum ſolúmque lumen: lumen, inquam, nōn magnitudine menſuratum, nōn coarctante figura aliqua circumſcriptum, nōn magnitudine tumidum, licet immenſum, ſed immenſurabile paſſim, tanquam omni menſura maius, omni quantitate præſtantius: ſi teipſum, inquam, id factum videris, viſus ipſe iam factus, atque teipſo fretus, eóque progreſſus, vt duce amplius indiceque non egeas: fige iam prorſus intuitum: ſolus namque hic oculus ingentem inſpicit pulchritudinem. At verò ſi fortè oculus vel ſordibus infectus, nec dum purgatus, vel ignauia debilis in ſpectaculum lucidiſſimū intendatur, caligabit protinus, nihilque diſcernet, vel ſi præſens quiſpiam ſpectaculum, quod alioquin cerni valeat, demōnſtrauerit. Oportet enim viſurū videndo cognatū ſimilemque prius efficere, quàm ad ſpectandū adhibeatur. Neque verò oculus vnquā videret ſolē, niſi factus ſolaris eſſet. Neque rurſus animus niſi factus ſit pulcher ipſam pulchritudinē intuebitur. Efficietur ergo diuinus, ſiue deiformis quilibet atque pulcher, ſi modò deum ſit & pulchritudinem inſpecturus. and indeed every way by which one can attain virtue: so that nothing else is left to them but to follow pleasure, and to attend only to their own affairs, and having abandoned the community of the human race, to pursue only their own utility: unless perhaps someone by his very nature is superior to such discourses. For of those things which are considered good and honorable among us, nothing is esteemed good among them, but something else, whatever they may at some time pursue. Although it was fitting for those who now know, to proceed from here, but those who follow should correct these first principles of ours, approaching these things from divine nature. For it belongs only to that nature which neglects bodily pleasure, to understand what is good and honorable. But those who are entirely devoid of virtue will in no way be able to ascend to higher things. This also provides testimony against them, that they make no mention of virtue, and entirely dismiss all discourse concerning those things which pertain to virtue: nor do they strive to define what virtue and the good are, or how many there are: and altogether whatever things, both excellent and numerous, are contained in the disputations of the ancients: nor again from what sources good things are acquired and possessed: nor in what manner the soul is cultivated and purified. For what they are accustomed to say, 'look to God,' is of no use at all: unless they clearly teach in what manner one is to look. For one might say that nothing prevents someone from looking indeed, yet not abstaining from any pleasure, nor restraining anger: and merely invoking the name of God itself, meanwhile succumbing to all disturbances, and not striving to repel them. Virtue, indeed acquired through prudence, and having progressed to the highest degree, shows God to us: but if anyone pronounces God without true virtue, he has nothing but the name.
Let no one think that he will become good by this very fact, that he despises the world, and the gods who reign in the world, and the other good and excellent things of the world. For every evil person has this primarily, that he despises the gods: nor is anyone entirely evil before he despises the heavenly beings. And if he is not yet evil in all other respects, yet from this one thing alone he becomes evil in all. Therefore, what they say, that they worship intelligible gods, has nothing consistent or akin to it. For whoever loves something, pursues with affection whatever is akin to that which he loves. For you also love the children of him whose father you love. But every soul is a daughter of that father. And the souls in the spheres of the world are intellectual and good, and much more akin to the heavenly beings than ours. For in what way would this world be separated from that, and in what way also the gods who are in the world? But concerning these things we have also spoken in earlier [parts]. But now it must be affirmed that those who despise the kin of the higher divinities do not even know those divinities, but apprehend them only by words. Moreover, what they say, that providence does not reach [the world], how can that be pious? Likewise, how is it entirely consistent with themselves? For they assert that the care of God is only for humans. But whether of humans, only while they are there, or also on earth

Quanquam decebat eos qui iam nouerint, hinc iam proſequi, ſequentes autem prima hæc noſtra corrigere ex diuina natura ad hæc accedentes. Illius namque naturæ duntaxat, quæ bonū honeſtumque ſit, intelligere. <margin>οὐδὲ</margin> Qui autem virtutis expertes ſunt omninò, nullo modo ad ſuperna accedere poterunt. Teſtimonium id quoque his adhibet, quòd nullum faciūt de virtute verbum, ſermonemque omnem de his quæ ad virtutem pertinent, omnino dimittunt: neque definire ſtudent, quid virtus & bonum, quotve ſint: & omnino quæcunq; tam præclara quàm multa priſcorum diſputationibus cōtinentur: neque rurſus ex quibus acquirantur bona atq; poſsideantur: neque quo pacto animus excolatur atque purgetur. <margin>δὴ προύργου εἴη</margin> Quod enim ſolent dicere, ad deum aſpice, nihil prodeſt omnino: niſi quo pacto inſpecturus ſis, perſpicuè doceant. Α καὶ ὅλως, <margin>* καθ' ἃ.</margin> * καθ' ἃ ἀπεδόθη ἄνθρωπος αὑτὸν οἴοιτο, ὥστε αὐτοὺς καταλείπεσθαι τὴν ἡδονὴν καὶ τὸ περὶ αὐτὰς, καὶ τὸ κοινὸν πρὸς ἄλλους ἀνθρώπους καὶ τὸ χρείας μόνον, εἰ μή τις τῇ φύσει τῇ αὐτῇ κρείττων εἴη τῶν λόγων τούτων. τῶν γὰρ οὐδὲν ἐν αὐτοῖς καλὸν ἀλλὰ ἄλλο τι, ὁπότε μεταδιώκουσι, καίτοι ἐχρῆν τοὺς ἤδη ἐγνωκότας εὐθὺς ὅθεν διώκειν· διώκοντας δὲ, πρῶτα κατορθοῦν ταῦτα ἐκ θείας φύσεως ἥκοντας· ἐκείνης γὰρ τῆς φύσεως καὶ τὸ ἐπιεικὲς, καὶ τὸ συνιέναι τῶν σώματος ἀτιμαζούσης, οἷς δὲ ἀρετῆς μὴ μέτεστιν, οὐκ ἂν εἶεν τὸ παράπαν κινηθέντες πρὸς ἐκεῖνα. μαρτυρεῖ δὲ αὐτοῖς καὶ τόδε, τὸ μηδένα λόγον περὶ ἀρετῆς πεποιῆσθαι, ἐκλελοιπέναι δὲ παντάπασι τὸν περὶ τούτων λόγον, καὶ μήτε τί ἐστιν εἰπεῖν, μήτε πόσα, μήτε ὅσα τεθεώρηται πολλὰ καὶ καλὰ παρὰ τῶν παλαιῶν λόγοις, μήτε ἐξ ὧν περιγίνεται, καὶ κτῆται· μήτε ὡς θεραπεύεται ψυχή· μήτε ὡς καθαίρεται. τὸ γὰρ δὴ εἰπεῖν, βλέπε πρὸς θεὸν, προύργου τί ἐργάζεται, ἐὰν μὴ πῶς καὶ βλέπῃ, διδάξῃ. τί γὰρ κωλύει, εἴποι τις ἂν, βλέπειν, εἰ μηδεμιᾶς ἀπεχέσθαι ἡδονῆς, ἢ ἀκρατῆ θυμοῦ εἶναι· μεμνημένον μὲν ὀνόματος, τῷ δὲ θεῷ συνεχόμενον δὲ ἀπὸ τῶν παθῶν, μηδὲν δὲ αὐτῶν πειρώμενον ἐξαιρεῖν; ἀρετὴ μὲν οὖν εἰς τέλος προβᾶσα, καὶ τῇ ψυχῇ ἐγγενομένη μετὰ φρονήσεως, θεὸν δείκνυσιν· ἄνευ δὲ ἀρετῆς ἀληθινῆς θεὸς λεγόμενον, ὄνομά ἐστι.

<margin>520</margin>
managing the citizens by both persuasion and compulsion, bringing them to share with one another the benefit that each is capable of contributing to the common good, and fostering such men in the city, not so that he may leave them to turn wherever each pleases, but so that he himself may use them for the binding together of the city.
<margin>5</margin>
True, he said, I had forgotten.

Consider then, I said, Glaucon, that we will not be doing an injustice to the philosophers who arise among us, but will be speaking justly to them, compelling them to oversee and guard the others. We will say that those who become such in other
<margin>b</margin>
cities reasonably do not share in the labors of those cities. For they grow up spontaneously against the will of the government in each, and it is just that the self-taught, owing no nourishment to anyone, should not be eager to pay the price of their nurture to anyone.
<margin>5</margin>
But we have brought you forth, both for yourselves and for the rest of the city, like leaders and kings in hives, having educated you better and more completely than those others, and more
<margin>c</margin>
capable of sharing in both ways of life. Therefore, each of you must in turn descend into the common dwelling of the others and grow accustomed to seeing the dark. For once accustomed, you will see ten thousand times better than those who are there, and you will know each of the images, what it is and of what, because you have seen the truth concerning the beautiful, the just, and the good. And so, the city will be inhabited by us and by you in wakefulness, not in a dream as most are now, inhabited by people fighting over shadows and quarreling with one another about ruling
<margin>d</margin>
as if it were some great good. But the truth is surely this: in a city where those who are to rule are least eager to rule, that city must of necessity be governed best and with the least faction, and one that has the opposite kind of rulers will be governed in the opposite way.

Entirely so, he said.

Will our pupils then disobey us, do you think, when they hear this?

Σκέψαι τοίνυν, εἶπον, ὦ Γλαύκων, ὅτι οὐδ’ ἀδικήσομεν τοὺς παρ’ ἡμῖν φιλοσόφους γιγνομένους, ἀλλὰ δίκαια πρὸς αὐτοὺς ἐροῦμεν, προσαναγκάζοντες τῶν ἄλλων ἐπιμελεῖσθαί τε καὶ φυλάττειν. ἐροῦμεν γὰρ ὅτι οἱ μὲν ἐν ταῖς ἄλλαις
<margin>b</margin>πόλεσι τοιοῦτοι γιγνόμενοι εἰκότως οὐ μετέχουσι τῶν ἐν αὐταῖς πόνων· αὐτόματοι γὰρ ἐμφύονται ἀκούσης τῆς ἐν ἑκάστῃ πολιτείας, δίκην δ’ ἔχει τό γε αὐτοφυὲς μηδενὶ τροφὴν ὀφείλον μηδ’ ἐκτίνειν τῳ προθυμεῖσθαι τὰ τροφεῖα·
<margin>5</margin>ὑμᾶς δ’ ἡμεῖς ὑμῖν τε αὐτοῖς τῇ τε ἄλλῃ πόλει ὥσπερ ἐν σμήνεσιν ἡγεμόνας τε καὶ βασιλέας ἐγεννήσαμεν, ἄμεινόν τε καὶ τελεώτερον ἐκείνων πεπαιδευμένους καὶ μᾶλλον δυ-
<margin>c</margin>νατοὺς ἀμφοτέρων μετέχειν. καταβατέον οὖν ἐν μέρει ἑκάστῳ εἰς τὴν τῶν ἄλλων συνοίκησιν καὶ συνεθιστέον τὰ σκοτεινὰ θεάσασθαι· συνεθιζόμενοι γὰρ μυρίῳ βέλτιον ὄψεσθε τῶν ἐκεῖ καὶ γνώσεσθε ἕκαστα τὰ εἴδωλα ἅττα
<margin>5</margin>ἐστὶ καὶ ὧν, διὰ τὸ τἀληθῆ ἑωρακέναι καλῶν τε καὶ δικαίων καὶ ἀγαθῶν πέρι. καὶ οὕτω ὕπαρ ἡμῖν καὶ ὑμῖν ἡ πόλις οἰκήσεται ἀλλ’ οὐκ ὄναρ, ὡς νῦν αἱ πολλαὶ ὑπὸ σκιαμαχούντων τε πρὸς ἀλλήλους καὶ στασιαζόντων περὶ τοῦ ἄρχειν
<margin>d</margin>οἰκοῦνται, ὡς μεγάλου τινὸς ἀγαθοῦ ὄντος. τὸ δέ που ἀληθὲς ὧδ’ ἔχει· ἐν πόλει ᾗ ἥκιστα πρόθυμοι ἄρχειν οἱ μέλλοντες ἄρξειν, ταύτην ἄριστα καὶ ἀστασιαστότατα ἀνάγκη οἰκεῖσθαι, τὴν δ’ ἐναντίους ἄρχοντας σχοῦσαν ἐναντίως.
<margin>5</margin>Πάνυ μὲν οὖν, ἔφη.
Ἀπειθήσουσιν οὖν ἡμῖν οἴει οἱ τρόφιμοι ταῦτ’ ἀκούοντες,

burnet_293.translation:
<header>REPUBLIC BOOK VII</header>

<page-num>517 d</page-num>
It is likely, he said.

What then? Do you think this is anything surprising, I said, if someone coming from divine contemplations to human evils behaves unseemly and appears very ridiculous, while still dim-sighted and before becoming sufficiently accustomed to the present darkness, being forced to struggle in courts of law or somewhere else about the shadows of justice, or the statues of which they are the shadows, and to dispute about this, in what way these things are assumed by those who have never seen justice itself?

It is not in the least surprising, he said.

But if a person had sense, I said, he would remember that disturbances of the eyes are twofold and arise from twofold causes, from light shifting to darkness and from darkness to light. And thinking that these same things happen also to the soul, whenever he sees one troubled and unable to see something clearly, he would not laugh irrationally, but would observe whether it has come from a brighter life and is darkened by lack of habit, or whether from greater ignorance it has moved into the brighter and is filled with the radiance of the light. And thus he would consider the one happy in its experience and life, and pity the other, and if he wished to laugh at it, his laughter would be less ridiculous than the laughter at the one coming down from the light above.

You speak quite reasonably, he said.

We must, I said, think this about them, if these things are true: that education is not what some who promise it say it is. For they say that they put knowledge into the soul where it is not present, as if they were putting sight into blind eyes.

For they do say that, he said.

Εἰκὸς μέντοι, ἔφη.

Τί δέ; τόδε οἴει τι θαυμαστόν, εἰ ἀπὸ θείων, ἦν δ᾽ ἐγώ, θεωριῶν ἐπὶ τὰ ἀνθρώπειά τις ἐλθὼν κακὰ ἀσχημονεῖ τε καὶ φαίνεται σφόδρα γελοῖος ἔτι ἀμβλυώττων καὶ πρὶν ἱκανῶς συνήθης γενέσθαι τῷ παρόντι σκότῳ ἀναγκαζόμενος ἐν δικαστηρίοις ἢ ἄλλοθί που ἀγωνίζεσθαι περὶ τῶν τοῦ δικαίου σκιῶν ἢ ἀγαλμάτων ὧν αἱ σκιαί, καὶ διαμιλλᾶσθαι περὶ τούτου, ὅπῃ ποτὲ ὑπολαμβάνεται ταῦτα ὑπὸ τῶν αὐτὴν δικαιοσύνην μὴ πώποτε ἰδόντων;

Οὐδ᾽ ὁπωστιοῦν θαυμαστόν, ἔφη.

Ἀλλ᾽ εἰ νοῦν γε ἔχοι τις, ἦν δ᾽ ἐγώ, μεμνῇτ᾽ ἂν ὅτι διτταὶ καὶ ἀπὸ διττῶν γίγνονται ἐπιταράξεις ὄμμασιν, ἔκ τε φωτὸς εἰς σκότος μεθισταμένων καὶ ἐκ σκότους εἰς φῶς. ταὐτὰ δὲ ταῦτα νομίσας γίγνεσθαι καὶ περὶ ψυχήν, ὁπότε ἴδοι θορυβουμένην τινὰ καὶ ἀδυνατοῦσάν τι καθορᾶν, οὐκ ἂν ἀλογίστως γελῷ, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπισκοποῖ ἂν πότερον ἐκ φανοτέρου βίου ἥκουσα ὑπὸ ἀηθείας ἐσκότωται, ἢ ἐξ ἀμαθίας πλείονος εἰς φανότερον ἰοῦσα ὑπὸ λαμπροτέρου μαρμαρυγῆς ἐμπέπλησται, καὶ οὕτω δὴ τὴν μὲν εὐδαιμονίσειεν ἂν τοῦ πάθους τε καὶ βίου, τὴν δὲ ἐλεήσειεν, καὶ εἰ γελᾶν ἐπ᾽ αὐτῇ βούλοιτο, ἧττον ἂν καταγέλαστος ὁ γέλως αὐτῷ εἴη ἢ ὁ ἐπὶ τῇ ἄνωθεν ἐκ φωτὸς ἡκούσῃ.

Καὶ μάλα, ἔφη, μετρίως λέγεις.

Δεῖ δή, εἶπον, ἡμᾶς τοιόνδε νομίσαι περὶ αὐτῶν, εἰ ταῦτ᾽ ἀληθῆ· τὴν παιδείαν οὐχ οἵαν τινὲς ἐπαγγελλόμενοί φασιν εἶναι τοιαύτην καὶ εἶναι. φασὶ δέ που οὐκ ἐνούσης ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ ἐπιστήμης σφεῖς ἐντιθέναι, οἷον τυφλοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς ὄψιν ἐντιθέντες.

Φασὶ γὰρ οὖν, ἔφη.
